topic: why home food photos look flat
caption:
Restaurants aren't using better cameras than you. They're using worse light, from a better direction.

Five fixes, none of which cost anything. Save this for your next dinner.
caption_fb: Restaurants aren't using better cameras than you — they're using worse light, from a better direction. Five fixes, none of which cost anything.
first_comment: The 45° one changes the most for the least effort. Try it tonight.

slides.headline: Your food looks flat. Theirs doesn't.
slides.subhead: It isn't the camera. It's *where the light is coming from* — and it's free to fix.
slides.alt: Cover: your food looks flat and theirs doesn't

slides.headline: You lit it from the front
slides.body: Front light fills every shadow, and shadow is the only thing that shows *texture*. Move the plate so the window is behind it, not behind you.
slides.alt: Front light removes the shadows that show texture

slides.headline: Turn the plate, not the camera
slides.body: Three-quarter back light rakes across the surface and brings back the grain, the crumb and the gloss.
slides.alt: Shoot at 45 degrees to the light source

slides.headline: Everything is the same height
slides.body: A flat plate photographs flat. Build one thing *taller* than the rest — a torn edge, a stacked slice, a spoon resting high.

slides.headline: Five fixes, in order
items: Put the window behind the plate

slides.quote: Gloss is just a reflection you remembered to aim.
slides.alt: Pull quote about gloss and reflections
